docs.title: Kubernetes, Helm, and the rest
docs.text: The same command as a pre-upgrade hook or an init step that runs before the migration Job, with restartPolicy: Never and backoffLimit: 0: a failed backup must fail the release, not retry until it happens to pass.

docs.title: Before the first deploy
docs.text:
• Run python manage.py check --deploy in the new image as part of your pipeline's test or build stage, against production settings if you can: E004 (a pg_dump older than the server) and E005/E006 (a bucket without Object Lock or its default rule) are better found there than at the deploy.
  • Make sure the CI job that runs your tests does not inherit the production notifier token — see Testing.
  • Run the deploy pass once by hand and restore it (Restore).

docs.title: Encryption and keys
docs.text:
'ENCRYPTION': {
    'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.encryption.age_cli.AgeCli',
    'RECIPIENTS': os.environ.get('BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT', ''),
},

Every object is encrypted with age to one or more public keys. The server holds only public keys, so it can write a backup and cannot read one. The private half lives off the machine — in your password manager, and nowhere else.

docs.title: Making a key pair
docs.text:
On your own machine, not the server:

age-keygen -o backup-acme-prod.key
# Public key: age1qyqszqgpqyqszqgpqyqszqgpqyqszqgpqyqszqgpqyqszqgpqyqs3290gq
  • The public key (age1…) goes into the server's environment, e.g. BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT. It is not a secret.
  • The file holds the private key (AGE-SECRET-KEY-1…). Put it in your password manager, then delete the file. age-keygen -y backup-acme-prod.key prints the public key again from it.

One key pair per product and environment keeps a leaked key's reach small. Losing the private key loses every backup sealed to it — store it where at least two people can reach it.

docs.title: RECIPIENTS
docs.text:
One public key, or a list. A comma-separated string is not split — read several from the environment yourself:

'RECIPIENTS': [r for r in os.environ.get('BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENTS', '').split(',') if r.strip()],

With several recipients, any one of the private keys opens a backup — a second key for a colleague, or a break-glass key in a safe.

age's SSH recipients (ssh-ed25519 …, ssh-rsa …) are accepted too.

manage.py check refuses anything else in RECIPIENTS as E008 — above all a private key, which would put the means to read every backup on the machine they protect:

?: (offsite_backup.E008) OFFSITE_BACKUP['ENCRYPTION']['RECIPIENTS'] holds a PRIVATE age key.
    HINT: Put the public half (age1...) here; the private half belongs off this machine.

docs.title: Compress, then encrypt
docs.text:
The order is not a preference: an encrypted stream does not compress. Databases and the configuration archive go source | zstd | age; media volumes go tar | age, because images and video are compressed already.

'COMPRESS': ['zstd', '-19', '--long=27', '-T0', '-q'],   # the default
'DECOMPRESS': ['zstd', '-d', '-q', '--long=31'],         # what a restore runs

-19 --long=27 is slow and small, which suits a batch job at night. A large database that does not finish in its window is better served by -10 than by no compression; an empty COMPRESS turns the stage off. DECOMPRESS must accept the window COMPRESS used — --long=31 accepts any. A restore decides whether to decompress from zstd's magic bytes, not from the name.

Every stage runs under pipefail semantics: a stage that dies mid-stream fails the pass instead of leaving a small, valid, truncated file.

docs.title: A second key for one dump: the wake identity
docs.text:
Some databases must be restorable by the server itself — a tenant put to sleep and woken on demand. Seal that one dump to an extra recipient whose private key the server holds, and keep every other backup readable off the machine only:

from offsite_backup import back_up_database, restore_database

key = back_up_database('tenant_42', extra_recipients=[settings.WAKE_RECIPIENT])
...
restore_database(key, 'tenant_42', identity=settings.WAKE_IDENTITY_FILE)

The server's wake key opens those dumps and nothing else. Treat it as a secret of the server, with the same care as its database password.

docs.title: Not in 0.1.0
docs.text: A pure-Python backend (pyrage, no age binary), an explicit "no encryption" backend, and helpers to re-seal recent backups to a new recipient are on the roadmap. For tests, offsite_backup.testing.Passthrough stands in for age — and raises W002 so it is never mistaken for encryption (Testing).

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
S3 + TelegramS3 + django-aiogramDirectory only 
pip install 'django-offsite-backup[s3,telegram]'

Backups in an S3 bucket with Object Lock, messages through the Telegram Bot API.

pip install 'django-offsite-backup[s3,aiogram]'

Messages through the bot your project already runs with django-aiogram; no token in these settings.

pip install django-offsite-backup

A local directory or Docker volume as the store, messages to the log. No driver at all — and no immutability either; see Stores: directory.

Requires Python 3.10–3.14 and Django 5.2+. Every pair in that range runs in CI, and an integration job runs a whole cycle — backup, restore into a clean database, row counts of every table compared — against PostgreSQL 16 and 18 and an S3 server with Object Lock.

docs.title: Extras
docs.text:
The base install is Django alone. Every backend is named by a dotted path in the settings, imported only when a pass first needs it, and its driver is an extra:

extra pulls for s3 boto3>=1.34 offsite_backup.stores.s3.S3Store, offsite_backup.media.s3.S3Source telegram httpx2>=2.16 offsite_backup.notifiers.telegram.TelegramNotifier aiogram django-aiogram>=5.2 offsite_backup.notifiers.django_aiogram.TopicNotifier all all of the above

Nothing is inferred from what happens to be installed. When a configured backend's driver is missing, manage.py check says so with the install line (E002):

?: (offsite_backup.E002) OFFSITE_BACKUP['STORE']['BACKEND'] is S3Store, but its driver is not installed.
    HINT: pip install "django-offsite-backup[s3]"

docs.title: Binaries
docs.text:
A pass streams through command-line tools rather than through Python memory. They are not Python dependencies; install them in the image that runs the backup:

binary needed for checked by pg_dump PostgresSource — its major version must be at least the server's E003, and E004 under check --deploy zstd COMPRESS (on by default) and DECOMPRESS (restoring) — whatever program they name E003 age AgeCli, both for sealing and for restoring E003 psql, pg_restore restoring a database (backup_restore --apply) and verifying a custom-format dump; shipped with pg_dump in every PostgreSQL client package E003

tar is not needed: volumes and the configuration archive are written with Python's tarfile. Measured on 613 MB in 2400 files, tarfile took 0.27 s against 0.72 s for the tar CLI, and it is the only option for media streamed from S3, which has no files on disk to hand to tar.

On Debian-based images:

RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends age zstd postgresql-common \
 && /usr/share/postgresql-common/pgdg/apt.postgresql.org.sh -y \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends postgresql-client-18 \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

Match postgresql-client-<N> to your server's major version, or newer: pg_dump refuses to dump a server newer than itself.

docs.title: Add the app
docs.text:
INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...,
    'offsite_backup',
]

The app registers the system checks and imports nothing else: no backend, no driver, no network until a pass runs. It has no models and no migrations.

docs.title: A first pass
docs.text:
1. Make a key pair on your machine, not the server, and keep the private half in your password manager (Encryption):

    age-keygen -o backup-acme-prod.key
# Public key: age1...

  2. Create the bucket with Object Lock, and a default COMPLIANCE rule of 13 days (S3 providers).

  3. Put the settings in settings.py, reading every credential from the environment (Settings):

    import os

OFFSITE_BACKUP = {
    'PREFIX': 'acme/prod',
    'ENV': 'prod',
    'STORE': {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.stores.s3.S3Store',
        'ENDPOINT_URL': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_ENDPOINT', ''),
        'REGION': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_REGION', ''),
        'BUCKET': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_BUCKET', ''),
        'ACCESS_KEY': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_ACCESS_KEY', ''),
        'SECRET_KEY': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_SECRET_KEY', ''),
    },
    'ENCRYPTION': {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.encryption.age_cli.AgeCli',
        'RECIPIENTS': os.environ.get('BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT', ''),
    },
    'DATABASES': {'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.databases.postgres.PostgresSource'},
    'CONFIG': {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.config.paths.PathsSource',
        'PATHS': ['/app/deploy'],
    },
    'NOTIFY': [
        {
            'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.notifiers.telegram.TelegramNotifier',
            'TOKEN': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_TOKEN', ''),
            'CHAT_ID': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID', ''),
        },
    ],
}

  4. Check, then run:

    python manage.py check
python manage.py check --deploy      # reaches the bucket and the database
python manage.py backup_offsite
# backup_offsite: 2 objects, 18734112 bytes up

  5. Restore it once, now, before you need to — Restore.

Then schedule the nightly pass and the morning check (Scheduling) and put the deploy pass in front of your migrations (Deploy integration).

docs.title: Media
docs.text:
'MEDIA': [
    {'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.media.filesystem.DirectorySource'},
],

Uploaded files, whatever holds them, packed into volumes of whole files.

docs.title: Where the media lives
Volumes
docs.text:
Media goes up in volumes of at most VOLUME_BYTES (4 GiB by default):

acme/prod/media/2026-03-10T03-00Z.001.tar.age
acme/prod/media/2026-03-10T03-00Z.002.tar.age
acme/prod/media/2026-03-10T03-00Z.003.tar.age
  • Whole files only. Each volume is a complete tar on its own: losing one loses its files, not the night, and any one of them restores with tar -x.
  • A file larger than a volume gets a volume of its own.
  • The budget counts tar's overhead: 20 KiB per volume (the end-of-archive blocks and the padding to a record) and 2 KiB per file (a 512-byte header, padding to 512, and a PAX header for a long or non-ASCII name), so a volume of many small files stays under the limit.
  • Streamed, one at a time: source → tar → age → disk → upload → delete, then the next volume. The workspace needs room for one sealed volume, not for the media; media larger than the free disk works.
  • Why 4 GiB: one S3 PUT stops at 5 GB. Volumes above 64 MiB go up multipart anyway, but a volume small enough for one PUT is the one that never surprises anyone. VOLUME_BYTES must be more than 20 KiB and at most 5 GB (E001).

Volumes are written with Python's tarfile in PAX format — measured faster than the tar CLI (0.27 s against 0.72 s on 613 MB in 2400 files), and the only option when the files come from S3. Each member is written with mode 0644 and the file's modification time; the size is taken when the file is opened, so a file that changed since it was listed is archived as it is now.

Not compressed by default. Images, video and PDFs are already compressed; zstd would spend the night gaining nothing. COMPRESS: True on a source runs the global COMPRESS stage on its volumes as well, and the suffix becomes .tar.zst.age.

docs.title: Filters
docs.text:
INCLUDE and EXCLUDE are lists of shell globs matched against each file's name inside the archive (fnmatch: * matches across / too). With INCLUDE, only matching names are kept; then anything matching EXCLUDE is left out:

'EXCLUDE': ['*.tmp', 'cache/*', '*/thumbs/*'],   # regenerable, not worth a night's upload

For S3Source the name includes PREFIX — write 'private/media/cache/*', or narrow PREFIX instead.

docs.title: Several sources
docs.text:
MEDIA is a list. Each source is a kind of its own, with its own volumes and its own rotation; give each a NAME:

'MEDIA': [
    {'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.media.filesystem.DirectorySource', 'ROOT': '/app/media'},
    {'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.media.filesystem.DirectorySource', 'ROOT': '/app/private', 'NAME': 'private'},
],

acme/prod/media/...
acme/prod/media-private/...

A single block instead of a list is accepted too.

docs.title: Empty is not an error
docs.text: A source with no files writes no volume, and the message says how many objects went up. The morning check does not depend on media: tonight's media does not stand in for a database that was not written.

docs.title: Leaving media out of one pass
docs.text: backup_offsite --without-media (or --only db --only config) writes the databases and the configuration only, and — in a project that has MEDIA configured — marks every object .without-media.: the pass a deploy runs. Those objects never count as a night; see Retention and Deploy integration.

docs.title: Not in 0.1.0
docs.text: A Docker volume not mounted where the backup runs (through the Docker API), any Django storage backend, and a manifest per volume for restoring one folder without downloading everything are on the roadmap.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: A failed pass says so. The night that never ran — the scheduler stopped, the worker was never deployed, the machine was off — says nothing at all. The morning check is the answer to that silence.

docs.title: The morning check
docs.text:
python manage.py backup_check
# backup_check: ok, newest whole backup 2026-03-10 03:00 UTC

It asks the store for the newest whole backup under:

  • the config/ folder, when CONFIG is set, and
  • every database's folder — db/, db-<alias>/ for each alias the pass would dump today,
  • or, with neither configured, every media folder.

Objects marked .without-media. do not count: a deploy at noon cannot stand in for a night that never ran. Media does not count either while there are databases or a configuration: tonight's media does not stand in for a database that was not written.

finding message exit every folder has a whole backup within STALE_HOURS (26) none 0 some folder's newest is older, or there is none MISSING, naming the oldest non-zero (BackupMissingError) the store could not be read UNCHECKED — as loud as missing non-zero (BackupUncheckedError) backups are off on this machine none 0, "nothing to do"

The error names every stale folder:

CommandError: backup_check: No whole backup within 26 h under acme/prod/: db-analytics/ (none), config/ (2026-03-08 03:00 UTC)

STALE_HOURS is 26 so that a pass at 03:00 one night and a slow one the next still pass a check at 09:00. Raise it if your nightly pass runs less often than daily.

Note that the database list is computed: with ALIASES a callable, a database added today is reported missing until its first nightly pass.

Schedule it as in Scheduling; from Python it is offsite_backup.check_last_night(), which returns the oldest of the newest whole backups (or None where backups are off) and raises the same errors.

docs.title: The last-success file
docs.text:
'LAST_SUCCESS_FILE': '/var/run/acme/backup-last-success',

After every successful pass the file is rewritten with the pass's time in ISO format:

2026-03-10T03:00:12.402113+00:00

Something already watching the machine can read its age — a node-exporter textfile collector, a Docker healthcheck, a monitoring agent's file-age check. It is written by every successful pass, deploy passes and passes by hand included, so it answers "did anything succeed lately", not "did last night run"; the morning check answers that. A file that cannot be written is logged (Last-success marker not written) and does not fail the pass. Mount the path where your monitor can see it — the worker writes it at night, the deploy's one-off container before a migration.

A metrics endpoint is on the roadmap.

docs.title: The log
docs.text:
Everything is logged to the offsite_backup logger, with fields in the record's extra (prefixed ob_, so a JSON formatter can keep them apart from your own):

level message fields INFO Backup written ob_prefix, ob_objects, ob_bytes INFO Database backed up (a one-off backup) ob_alias, ob_key INFO Nightly backup skipped: ... (off, done, or being done) — ERROR (with traceback) Database not backed up ob_alias WARNING Backup still locked; left for a later night ob_key, ob_until WARNING Backup depth not read ob_folder WARNING Last-success marker not written ob_path, ob_error WARNING Media file not listed, Media file not readable; left out ob_path, ob_error ERROR Notifier not built, Notifier raised ob_notifier, ob_error ERROR Backup message not formatted ob_error ERROR Telegram refused the backup message ob_status, ob_description ERROR Telegram unreachable, Backup message not sent through the bot ob_error (the class only) INFO / ERROR Backup written / Backup failed ... from LogNotifier ob_prefix, ob_text

No message, token, password or private key is ever logged.

docs.title: What the store holds
docs.text: python manage.py backup_list prints, per kind, the nights kept, the oldest night, the objects and bytes, the newest stamp, how long the newest object is locked and how many objects came from passes without media. --json for scripts. See Restore.

docs.title: Notifications
docs.text:
'NOTIFY': [
    {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.notifiers.telegram.TelegramNotifier',
        'TOKEN': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_TOKEN', ''),
        'CHAT_ID': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID', ''),
        'TOPIC_ID': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_TOPIC_ID', ''),
    },
],

Every outcome — written, failed, missing, unchecked — is said where a person reads it. NOTIFY is a list; every notifier in it gets every message.

docs.title: What the messages look like
docs.text:
HTML, written to be read on a phone among everything else in the chat: the first line is what happened and where, the second why it ran, figures one per line, hashtags last — so a thread of them is searchable by kind, and a failure never looks like the hundred successes around it.

WrittenFailedMissingUnchecked 
💾 Backup written: acme/prod
🌙 Nightly

📦 Objects: 7
⚖️ Size: 5312.4 MB
⏱ Took: 1044s
🗄 Kept: 14 days, since 2026-02-25
🧹 Past the window: 7 removed

#backup #prod #nightly #ok

Kept is left out when the depth could not be read; Past the window when nothing was removed. A pass without media adds 🖼 Media: left to the nightly pass.

🚨 Backup FAILED: acme/prod
🚀 Before a deploy
The deploy stops here; the live release keeps serving.

1 database(s) not backed up, the rest went up — default: PipelineError: `pg_dump` exited with status 1: pg_dump: error: aborting because of server version mismatch

#backup #prod #deploy #failed

The error is cut at 500 characters. The deploy line appears only for --reason deploy.

🚨 Backup MISSING: acme/prod
🕘 Morning check

Newest backup: 2026-03-09 03:00 UTC, 30 h ago
Expected within 26 h

#backup #prod #missing

🚨 Backups UNCHECKED: acme/prod
🕘 Morning check: the store could not be read

ClientError: An error occurred (InvalidAccessKeyId) ...

#backup #prod #missing

As loud as missing, on purpose: a check that could not look has not seen a backup.

The second line comes from --reason:

reason line hashtag nightly 🌙 Nightly #nightly deploy 🚀 Before a deploy #deploy manual (the command's default), by hand ✋ By hand #manual upgrade ⬆️ Before an upgrade #upgrade anything else 🔁 Reason #reason, non-alphanumerics replaced by _

Every interpolated value is escaped. A chat rejects a message whose HTML does not parse, and an error text with a < in it would otherwise be lost silently.

docs.title: Telegram
docs.text:
pip install 'django-offsite-backup[telegram]' — the Bot API over HTTPS with httpx2.

option TOKEN, CHAT_ID required TOPIC_ID a forum topic (message_thread_id); empty for the main thread TIMEOUT seconds, default 10 API_URL default https://api.telegram.org; for a local Bot API server
  • A topic id typed wrong makes Telegram refuse the message. It is logged (Telegram refused the backup message, with Telegram's description) and nothing is posted to the main thread instead.
  • A 429 is retried once after Telegram's retry_after, if that is 30 seconds or less.
  • Neither the token nor the text is ever logged. A connection error is logged by its class only — the URL, and so the token, is in the message of several of them.

docs.title: Through django-aiogram
docs.text:
pip install 'django-offsite-backup[aiogram]' — the project's own bot, configured where django-aiogram is; no token here.

'NOTIFY': [
    {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.notifiers.django_aiogram.TopicNotifier',
        'CHAT_ID': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID', ''),
        'TOPIC_ID': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_TOPIC_ID', ''),
        # 'BOT': 'ops',   # one of TELEGRAM_BOTS; the default bot when absent
    },
],

It calls bot.send_raw('send_message', ...), which talks to Telegram from the calling process — synchronously where no bot loop runs (a Celery worker, a one-off deploy container). In a process whose bot loop is running, send_raw only schedules the call, and "delivered" means "handed over". Whether a refused send raises follows django-aiogram's own RAISE_EXCEPTION; either way this notifier logs it and the backup goes on.

docs.title: The log
docs.text:
'NOTIFY': [{'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.notifiers.log.LogNotifier'}],

Writes to the offsite_backup logger: INFO for a written backup, ERROR for anything else, the text in the record's ob_text extra field. It reaches no network, so it keeps working under tests.

docs.title: A notifier never costs the backup
docs.text: Every send is wrapped: a notifier that raises, times out or is misconfigured is logged (Notifier raised, Notifier not built) and the pass goes on. A notifier outage never turns a written backup into a failed one, and never hides a real failure behind its own. The exit status of the command is the pass's, not the chat's.

docs.title: Tests never notify
docs.text: The package's pytest plugin and OffsiteBackupTestRunner silence every notifier that can reach the network for the whole test run, whatever the environment holds. See Testing.

docs.title: Your own notifier
docs.text:
from offsite_backup.notifiers.base import Notifier


class SlackNotifier(Notifier):
    REQUIRED = ('WEBHOOK_URL',)

    def send(self, outcome, text):
        try:
            ...  # post text; outcome.kind is 'written', 'failed', 'missing' or 'unchecked'
        except Exception:
            return False
        return True

send() must not raise and answers whether the message was delivered. Leave REACHES_NETWORK = True (the default) for anything that leaves the process, so tests silence it.

docs.title: Your own format
docs.text:
MESSAGES is a dotted path to a callable taking an Outcome and returning the text, or to a module holding one called format_outcome:

OFFSITE_BACKUP = {..., 'MESSAGES': 'acme.backups.format_outcome'}

offsite_backup.outcome.Outcome carries kind, prefix, env, name, reason, summary (objects uploaded, bytes, seconds, removed, failed databases, depth), error, and for the morning check newest, stale_hours and now. A formatter that raises is logged (Backup message not formatted) and nothing is sent — the outcome itself still stands. offsite_backup.messages.default is the reference; its reason_line() and reason_tag() are reusable.

docs.title: Restore
docs.text: A backup nobody has restored is a hope. This page is the procedure, and a drill to run every month so the procedure is known to work before the day it is needed.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• The private key — from your password manager. Never copy it to the production server for a routine restore; restore from your own machine, or from a throwaway one.
  • A machine with the project's image (or a checkout with the package installed), age, zstd, and psql/pg_restore of the server's major version or newer.
  • Settings that point at the same store and PREFIX. A read-only S3 key is enough and better than the server's.

The private key is given as a file (--identity FILE) or in the AGE_IDENTITY environment variable — never as an argument, which ps would show. From the variable it is written to a 0600 file in a private temporary directory for age, and removed with it.

docs.title: 1. See what there is
docs.text:
python manage.py backup_list

acme/prod/
  config/: 14 nights since 2026-02-25, 19 objects, 0.4 MB, newest 2026-03-10T14-12Z, locked until 2026-03-23T14:12:31+00:00, 5 without media
  db/: 14 nights since 2026-02-25, 19 objects, 410.2 MB, newest 2026-03-10T14-12Z, locked until 2026-03-23T14:12:31+00:00, 5 without media
  media/: 14 nights since 2026-02-25, 28 objects, 74322.0 MB, newest 2026-03-10T03-00Z, locked until 2026-03-23T03:02:10+00:00

--kind db narrows it (repeat for several); --json is for scripts.

docs.title: 2. Download and decrypt
docs.text:
export AGE_IDENTITY="$(cat ~/secure/backup-acme-prod.key)"      # or --identity FILE
python manage.py backup_restore --stamp latest --into ./restore

restore/config/2026-03-10T03-00Z.tar
restore/db/2026-03-10T03-00Z.sql  (verified)
restore/media/2026-03-10T03-00Z.001.tar
restore/media/2026-03-10T03-00Z.002.tar
  • --stamp latest is the newest whole backup (the newest night in config/, or in db/ without a configuration archive); a pass without media is not "whole". Give a stamp such as --stamp 2026-03-10T14-12Z to take any pass, a deploy's included.
  • Every object of that stamp is downloaded, decrypted and — if it starts with zstd's magic bytes — decompressed, into <into>/<kind>/. --into defaults to ./restore-<stamp>.
  • --kind db (repeatable) takes only some kinds — skip a night's media when you need the database.
  • Every database dump is verified: a plain dump must end with PostgreSQL database dump complete; a custom-format one must pass pg_restore --list. A dump that fails says so and stops.
  • Backups copied under <PREFIX>/released/ are not part of a stamp; restore those with --apply and the full key (below).

What you get:

kind file open with db, db-<alias> <stamp>.sql (plain) or <stamp>.dump (custom) psql, pg_restore media, media-<name> <stamp>.<NNN>.tar, one per volume tar -xf — each volume on its own config <stamp>.tar tar -xf; rendered.env is the environment

docs.title: 3. Load a database
docs.text:
python manage.py backup_restore --stamp latest --apply --database default
  • --apply --database ALIAS downloads, decrypts, verifies and loads the dump into that DATABASES alias — with psql --single-transaction for plain SQL, pg_restore --single-transaction --exit-on-error for the custom format, both --no-owner.
  • With --apply, --stamp latest means the newest dump of that database, a deploy's included — the most recent state is what you want back.
  • --stamp also takes a full key: --stamp acme/prod/released/db-tenant_42/2026-03-01T10-00Z.sql.zst.age.

  • --from-database ALIAS loads another alias's backup — production's default into a scratch database:

    python manage.py backup_restore --stamp latest --apply --database scratch --from-database default

  • The target must be empty. --clean replaces a non-empty one: it runs DROP SCHEMA public CASCADE; CREATE SCHEMA public; first. Objects in other schemas are not dropped.

From Python:

from offsite_backup import restore_database

restore_database('latest', 'scratch', identity='~/secure/backup-acme-prod.key', source_alias='default')
restore_database('2026-03-10T03-00Z', 'default', clean=True)  # identity from AGE_IDENTITY

restore_database(source, alias, *, identity=None, clean=False, source_alias=None) answers with the key it loaded.

docs.title: 4. Media and configuration
docs.text:
mkdir -p media && for v in restore/media/*.tar; do tar -xf "$v" -C media; done
mkdir -p deploy && tar -xf restore/config/*.tar -C deploy

Names in a media volume are relative to the source's ROOT (or are the full object keys, for an S3 source). Copy them back into the volume, directory or bucket the application reads. rendered.env is the environment the release ran with — the file to rebuild .env from on a new machine.

docs.title: Rebuilding a lost machine
docs.text:
1. Provision the machine; install Docker.
  2. backup_restore --stamp latest --into ./restore on your own machine.
  3. Unpack the configuration archive and copy its deployment directory to the new machine; rebuild .env from rendered.env (and rotate any secret you suspect left with the old machine).
  4. Start the database; backup_restore --stamp latest --apply --database default from inside the new deployment, with AGE_IDENTITY set for that one command only — or load the dump you already decrypted in step 2 with psql/pg_restore, and the private key never touches the server.
  5. Unpack the media volumes into the media volume or bucket.
  6. Start the application; run backup_offsite --reason manual and check the message.

docs.title: The monthly drill
docs.text:
Restoring is a skill that decays. Once a month, on a calendar reminder:

  1. Take the newest whole backup: backup_restore --stamp latest --into ./drill. Note the stamp and that every dump says (verified).

  2. Start a clean PostgreSQL of the same major as production:

    docker run -d --name drill -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=drill -p 55432:5432 postgres:18

  3. Load the dump into it, either with psql/pg_restore directly or with an extra alias (DATABASES['drill']) and backup_restore --stamp <stamp> --apply --database drill --from-database default.

  4. Count every table in both databases and compare:

    SELECT format('SELECT %L AS t, count(*) FROM %I.%I', table_name, table_schema, table_name)
FROM information_schema.tables
WHERE table_schema = 'public' AND table_type = 'BASE TABLE'
ORDER BY table_name \gexec

    Production keeps changing, so expect the newest rows to differ; every table present, and counts close, is the pass mark. For a custom-format dump, also compare the entry count of pg_restore --list. 5. Unpack one media volume and open a few files. 6. Unpack the configuration archive and read rendered.env — is every variable the application needs there? 7. Write down the date, the stamp, the table count and how long it took. Delete the drill database and ./drill.

An automated drill command — restore the newest backup into a throwaway database, count rows per table against the live one, report to the same chat — is on the roadmap.

docs.title: Retention and locks
docs.text:
'RETENTION': {'KEEP_NIGHTS': 14},
'STORE': {..., 'LOCK_DAYS': 13},

Each kind keeps its newest 14 whole nights; every object is locked for 13 days. One less, on purpose.

docs.title: Counted in whole nights
docs.text:
Retention counts calendar nights in UTC, read from the object's name — not objects, and not age:

  • not objects, because a night's media is several volumes, and a night with ten volumes would otherwise push out nine nights of databases;
  • not stamps, because a project runs several passes a day — the nightly one, one per deploy, one by hand — and counting each would push out nights whose lock still holds;
  • not the store's timestamps, because the name is what a person reads in a listing and what every store keeps the same way.

2026-03-10T03-00Z and 2026-03-10T14-12Z are one night: 2026-03-10. A key whose name carries no stamp is not a backup and is never touched.

Each kind folder rotates on its own — db/, db-analytics/, media/, config/ — and strictly inside <PREFIX>/<kind>/, with the trailing slash: db/ never matches db-analytics/, and acme/prod/ never matches acme/prod-old/. A pass rotates the kinds it wrote to, so a nightly pass rotates media and a deploy pass does not.

docs.title: Rotation runs last
docs.text: Only after every part of the pass is uploaded. Making room before the new backup exists is how a bad night becomes an empty bucket. A pass that failed before the end — an upload, a lock read-back, a media volume — rotates nothing. A pass in which only a database dump failed does rotate; the failed database's folder simply has no new night, so it keeps its newest 14 as before.

docs.title: Passes without media
docs.text:
A deploy pass writes the databases and the configuration and leaves the media to the night. Its objects are marked .without-media.:

acme/prod/db/2026-03-10T14-12Z.without-media.sql.zst.age

Those objects never count as nights. They are kept while they are newer than the oldest whole night kept, and deleted with it. Counted naively, a fortnight of deploys over failing nights would push out the last whole backup's database while its media stayed — unrestorable.

With no whole night at all — a fresh setup that has seen only deploys — partial nights are counted by themselves, so the folder cannot grow without bound.

The marker is written only in a project that has MEDIA configured. Where there is no media, a pass without media is a whole backup, and counts as one.

docs.title: Versions and delete markers
docs.text: On a versioned bucket, deleting a key without a version id only writes a delete marker: the bytes stay stored and billed. Rotation therefore lists every version of every key in the folder — markers included — and deletes each by version id. An expired key leaves nothing behind.

docs.title: Locks: why one day less
docs.text:
A COMPLIANCE lock cannot be shortened or removed by anyone until it runs out — that is its point. Rotation deletes the 15th-newest night; with 13-day locks, everything it reaches is unlocked already. E007 refuses KEEP_NIGHTS <= LOCK_DAYS:

?: (offsite_backup.E007) RETENTION['KEEP_NIGHTS'] is 13, not more than OFFSITE_BACKUP['STORE']['LOCK_DAYS'] = 13.
    HINT: Keep at least one night more than the lock (e.g. 14 nights, 13 days), so rotation only ever deletes objects whose lock has run out.

A version that is still locked when rotation reaches it — a night of several passes, a clock that disagrees — is left for a later night with a warning in the log (Backup still locked; left for a later night), not a failure: a refused delete must not fail the night over an object that is safe.

Changing either number:

  • more nights — raise KEEP_NIGHTS and leave LOCK_DAYS;
  • longer locks — raise LOCK_DAYS, change the bucket's default rule to the same number (E006), and keep KEEP_NIGHTS above it (E007). Objects already written keep the lock they were given.

docs.title: Depth
docs.text:
After rotation the pass reads how far back the backups reach — the number of distinct nights under the first database's folder (the configuration's, without databases) whose current version is an object, and the oldest of them:

🗄 Kept: 14 days, since 2026-02-25

The count includes nights that only a deploy pass wrote. It is best effort: a depth that cannot be read is a line left out of the message, never a failed backup.

docs.title: Storage, roughly
docs.text: A kind holds about KEEP_NIGHTS nights of whole backups plus every deploy pass since the oldest of them. Media is uploaded whole every night, so it dominates: 5 GB of media at 14 nights is about 70 GB stored. Incremental media is on the roadmap, for when that stops being acceptable.

docs.title: S3 providers
docs.text:
Whatever the provider, the bucket needs three things, and the first one is only possible at creation:

  1. Object Lock, enabled when the bucket is created (versioning comes with it);
  2. a default retention rule of COMPLIANCE, LOCK_DAYS days — 13 unless you changed it;
  3. a key for the backup alone.

Then python manage.py check --deploy on the server: no E005, no E006, and the bucket is ready. Run a first pass with media (volumes go up multipart, which is what the default rule is for) and look for Backup written before trusting it.

The examples use the AWS CLI, which talks to every provider below with --endpoint-url.

docs.title: Hetzner Object Storage
docs.text:
The provider this package's S3 rules were measured on.

One Hetzner project per product or client. Hetzner's S3 credentials belong to a project and reach every bucket in it; they cannot be narrowed to a bucket or a prefix. A key leaked from one product's server must not open another's backups, so each product — and each client — gets its own project, its own bucket and its own key. Services of your own that share a trust boundary may share one bucket, a PREFIX each.

  1. Create the project, then the S3 credentials in it (Security → S3 credentials). The secret is shown once.

  2. Create the bucket with Object Lock. It cannot be enabled later; a bucket created without it has to be replaced. With the AWS CLI:

    export AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID=... AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY=...
ENDPOINT=https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com     # nbg1, hel1, ... — the bucket's location

aws s3api create-bucket --bucket acme-backups \
    --object-lock-enabled-for-bucket --endpoint-url "$ENDPOINT"

    If you create it in the console instead, tick Object Lock in the creation dialog.

  3. Set the default rule — COMPLIANCE, days equal to LOCK_DAYS:

    aws s3api put-object-lock-configuration --bucket acme-backups --endpoint-url "$ENDPOINT" \
    --object-lock-configuration \
    '{"ObjectLockEnabled": "Enabled", "Rule": {"DefaultRetention": {"Mode": "COMPLIANCE", "Days": 13}}}'

aws s3api get-object-lock-configuration --bucket acme-backups --endpoint-url "$ENDPOINT"
aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket acme-backups --endpoint-url "$ENDPOINT"   # "Enabled"

  4. The settings:

    'STORE': {
    'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.stores.s3.S3Store',
    'ENDPOINT_URL': 'https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com',
    'REGION': 'fsn1',
    'BUCKET': 'acme-backups',
    'ACCESS_KEY': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_ACCESS_KEY', ''),
    'SECRET_KEY': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_SECRET_KEY', ''),
    'LOCK_DAYS': 13,
},

What was measured there, and what the package does about each — the reasoning is on Stores: S3:

  • a single PUT ignored the default rule and landed GOVERNANCE → the lock is an argument of every upload;
  • a multipart upload took its date from the default rule → the rule must equal LOCK_DAYS (E006), and every lock is read back;
  • a single PUT above 5 GB was refused → multipart in 64 MiB parts, volumes of 4 GiB;
  • there is no IAM to withhold "bypass governance" → COMPLIANCE only;
  • a delete without a version id only adds a marker → rotation deletes versions.

docs.title: AWS S3
docs.text:
Leave ENDPOINT_URL empty and set REGION.

aws s3api create-bucket --bucket acme-backups --region eu-central-1 \
    --create-bucket-configuration LocationConstraint=eu-central-1 \
    --object-lock-enabled-for-bucket

aws s3api put-object-lock-configuration --bucket acme-backups \
    --object-lock-configuration \
    '{"ObjectLockEnabled": "Enabled", "Rule": {"DefaultRetention": {"Mode": "COMPLIANCE", "Days": 13}}}'

AWS can narrow a key to a prefix, so several projects may share a bucket safely. A starting point for the backup user's policy — what a pass, the morning check, backup_list, keep_apart and a restore call, and nothing that changes the bucket:

{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:GetBucketVersioning", "s3:GetBucketObjectLockConfiguration"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-backups"
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["s3:ListBucket", "s3:ListBucketVersions"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-backups",
      "Condition": {"StringLike": {"s3:prefix": ["acme/prod/*"]}}
    },
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": [
        "s3:PutObject", "s3:PutObjectRetention", "s3:AbortMultipartUpload",
        "s3:GetObject", "s3:GetObjectVersion", "s3:GetObjectRetention",
        "s3:DeleteObjectVersion"
      ],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-backups/acme/prod/*"
    }
  ]
}

Do not grant s3:BypassGovernanceRetention, s3:PutBucketObjectLockConfiguration, s3:PutBucketVersioning or s3:DeleteBucket. A restore needs only the read actions, and is better done with a separate read-only key from your own machine.

docs.title: MinIO
docs.text:
The package's integration tests run against MinIO with Object Lock and versioning.

mc alias set backups https://minio.example.com "$ACCESS_KEY" "$SECRET_KEY"
mc mb --with-lock backups/acme-backups
mc retention set --default COMPLIANCE 13d backups/acme-backups
mc retention info --default backups/acme-backups

'STORE': {
    'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.stores.s3.S3Store',
    'ENDPOINT_URL': 'https://minio.example.com',
    'REGION': 'us-east-1',
    'BUCKET': 'acme-backups',
    ...
},

A MinIO on the same machine as the application is not off-site. Run it elsewhere, or treat it like a directory store.

docs.title: Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2 and others
docs.text:
Not yet verified. This package needs, from the S3 API:

  • PutObject and multipart uploads that accept ObjectLockMode and ObjectLockRetainUntilDate, and HeadObject that returns them;
  • GetObjectLockConfiguration with a default retention rule, and GetBucketVersioning;
  • ListObjectVersions with delete markers, and DeleteObject with a VersionId.

Check your provider's S3-compatibility documentation for each of these before relying on it. Then prove it on a throwaway bucket: manage.py check --deploy tells you what the bucket answers (E005, E006), and a pass with a media volume above 64 MiB tells you whether a multipart object lands with the date asked (BackupUnlockedError if not).

A provider that cannot lock objects can still hold backups with LOCK_DAYS: 0 — encrypted, off the machine, and deletable by the key on the server. Say so in your own runbook; the Security model explains what that gives up.

Reports of what works on other providers are welcome as issues.

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
Two jobs, both in UTC:

job when what the nightly pass 03:00 UTC everything, media included; guarded to once per night the morning check 09:00 UTC is there a whole backup younger than STALE_HOURS? — Monitoring

Object names, nights and the guard are all UTC, whatever TIME_ZONE says. Run the morning check a few hours after the pass, so a slow night is not reported missing, and early enough in your working day that someone reads it.

docs.title: Celery
docs.text:
# settings.py
from offsite_backup.schedule.celery import beat_schedule

CELERY_TIMEZONE = 'UTC'
CELERY_IMPORTS = ['offsite_backup.schedule.celery']
CELERY_BEAT_SCHEDULE = {
    **beat_schedule(),                 # nightly 03:00, check 09:00
    # **beat_schedule(nightly=(2, 30), check=(8, 0)),
    ...
}

offsite_backup.schedule.celery defines two shared tasks, offsite_backup.nightly (run_nightly()) and offsite_backup.check (check_last_night()), and beat_schedule(nightly=(3, 0), check=(9, 0)) returns beat entries for both as (hour, minute) crontabs in the beat's timezone — hence CELERY_TIMEZONE = 'UTC', or shift the hours. CELERY_IMPORTS makes sure the worker registers the tasks; this assumes the usual app.config_from_object('django.conf:settings', namespace='CELERY').

The module imports Celery, so only a project that runs Celery imports it.

The check task raises when a backup is missing or the store cannot be read, so the task fails wherever your Celery failures are reported, on top of the chat message.

docs.title: taskiq
docs.text:
# acme/broker.py
from taskiq import TaskiqScheduler
from taskiq.schedule_sources import LabelScheduleSource

from offsite_backup.schedule.taskiq import register

broker = ...  # your broker
backup_nightly, backup_check = register(broker)
# register(broker, nightly='30 2 * * *', check='0 8 * * *')

scheduler = TaskiqScheduler(broker, sources=[LabelScheduleSource(broker)])

register(broker, *, nightly='0 3 * * *', check='0 9 * * *') defines the same two tasks, named offsite_backup.nightly and offsite_backup.check, with schedule labels for taskiq's LabelScheduleSource (cron, UTC). The pass is a blocking batch job, so each task runs it in a thread. The worker must have Django set up before the tasks run, as for any task that touches the ORM.

docs.title: cron, systemd timers, Kubernetes CronJobs
docs.text:
Anything that runs a command on a schedule:

CRON_TZ=UTC
0 3 * * *  cd /app && python manage.py backup_offsite --reason nightly
0 9 * * *  cd /app && python manage.py backup_check

The command is not guarded (below) — cron fires once, so it does not need to be. Both commands exit non-zero on failure, so cron's mail, a systemd OnFailure= unit or the CronJob's failed status sees it as well as the chat.

With Docker Compose and a host crontab:

0 3 * * *  cd /srv/acme && docker compose exec -T worker python manage.py backup_offsite --reason nightly

docs.title: Once per night
docs.text:
A deploy that recreates the scheduler around the nightly time fired the nightly task twice — the old scheduler as it stopped, the new one as it started. Two passes in one night double the upload and race each other's rotation. So run_nightly() — what both adapters call — claims the UTC night in a Django cache every worker shares:

  1. a night already done is skipped;
  2. otherwise it claims running with an atomic cache.add (held for RUNNING_SECONDS, an hour); a night someone else is running is skipped;
  3. it looks for done again under the claim, in case it finished in between;
  4. on failure it releases the claim and re-raises, so the scheduler's retry can run tonight;
  5. on success it writes done (kept DONE_SECONDS, 26 hours — past the end of its UTC date) before releasing running, so there is no moment when neither is set.

A pass whose worker died holds the night for an hour at most. The keys are offsite_backup:<PREFIX>:<YYYY-MM-DD>:done and :running.

'GUARD': {'CACHE': 'default'},   # ENABLED True, RUNNING_SECONDS 3600, DONE_SECONDS 93600

The cache must be shared between the workers and the schedulers: Redis, Memcached, the database cache. A LocMemCache or DummyCache is per process and guards nothing; W003 says so. A CACHE alias missing from CACHES is E001. 'GUARD': {'ENABLED': False} turns the claim off.

Passes by hand and deploy passes are never guarded: they are meant to run whenever someone asks.

docs.title: Calling it yourself
docs.text:
from offsite_backup import run, run_nightly, check_last_night

run_nightly()  # guarded; None when skipped or when backups are off
run(reason='manual')  # one pass now; Summary, or raises
run(media=False, reason='deploy')
run(only=['db'])  # 'db', 'media', 'config'
check_last_night()  # oldest of the newest whole backups; raises when missing

run() raises NotConfiguredError on a machine where backups are off; the commands and run_nightly() check first and do nothing there.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text: The design goal in one line: the machine that writes a backup cannot read one, and cannot destroy one it has written. This page says how far that holds, and where it stops.

docs.title: What sits where
docs.text: where secret? age public key(s) server environment (RECIPIENTS) no age private key your password manager, off the machine yes — opens every backup S3 key for the store server environment yes — writes, lists, reads ciphertext S3 key for an S3 media source server environment yes — reads the media bucket notifier token server environment, or django-aiogram's settings yes database password server environment, PGPASSWORD for pg_dump yes a wake key (optional) server yes — opens only the dumps sealed to it

docs.title: What the server can and cannot do
docs.text:
The server — the application, its worker, anyone who has a shell on it — can:

  • write new backups, list the store, download ciphertext;
  • read the media, the databases, the deployment directory and the environment, because it backs them up;
  • stop backing up.

It cannot:

  • read a backup. Everything is sealed with age to public keys; the private key is not on the machine, and E008 refuses one in RECIPIENTS.
  • delete or shorten a COMPLIANCE-locked object before its lock runs out — not with the key it has — and, on providers that implement COMPLIANCE as AWS does, not with the account's root credentials either. That is what COMPLIANCE means, and why it is the only mode this package uses.
  • send backups somewhere else by accident. The S3 client is built from the configured options only; ambient credentials (~/.aws, instance roles, AWS_*) are ignored.

docs.title: A stolen store key (the server is compromised, or a key leaks)
docs.text:
• Cannot read backups: ciphertext only.
  • Cannot delete a locked object within its lock — 13 days by default. Deleting the key name only adds a delete marker; the locked version stays and can be retrieved by version id with the provider's tools.
  • Can add things on top: new versions of a key or delete markers. backup_restore reads the current version, so after a compromise list the versions (aws s3api list-object-versions) and restore from a version written before it. The morning check only sees current versions, so hiding the recent backups behind markers makes it report them missing.
  • Can delete what is no longer locked: everything older than LOCK_DAYS. The window you can count on after a compromise is LOCK_DAYS, not KEEP_NIGHTS. Notice early — that is what the morning check is for — and raise LOCK_DAYS (with the bucket's default rule and KEEP_NIGHTS) if two weeks is too short for you.
  • Can fill the bucket and so the bill. Provider-side quotas and billing alerts are the answer.
  • On a provider where keys reach every bucket of their project, can do all of the above to every bucket in that project. Hence one project per product or client (S3 providers).

docs.title: GOVERNANCE mode
docs.text: Bypassable by any key holding the "bypass governance retention" permission — on some providers, any key at all. It protects against mistakes, not against an attacker with the server's key. This package never uses it, and the read-back fails a pass where an object lands GOVERNANCE.

docs.title: A directory store
docs.text: No immutability. Anyone who can write to the directory can delete every backup in it, and it is on the machine it protects. It protects against a dropped table, not against a lost machine or an intruder (W001).

docs.title: LOCK_DAYS: 0
docs.text: The same as a directory store, off the machine: encrypted, and deletable by the server's key.

docs.title: The private key
docs.text: Whoever has it can read every backup sealed to it — including the configuration archive, which holds every secret the application has (rendered.env). Keep it off servers, keep it where two people can reach it, and restore from your own machine. If it ever reached a server, make a new pair and treat the old backups as exposed.

docs.title: The wake key
docs.text: A server that holds an extra identity can open the dumps sealed to it — by design, so it can restore them itself — and nothing else. Seal only the dumps that need it.

docs.title: What leaves the machine besides backups
docs.text:
• Messages carry the prefix, sizes, durations and, on failure, the first 500 characters of the error — escaped. Errors never include the database password: it travels in PGPASSWORD, never on a command line. A Telegram transport error is logged by its class only, because its text contains the URL and therefore the token.
  • No message, token, password or private key is logged.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Notifiers that reach the network are silenced for every pytest run and under OffsiteBackupTestRunner. Keep production tokens out of CI test jobs anyway (Testing).

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text: Please report security issues privately through GitHub's security advisories for the repository rather than in a public issue. See SECURITY.md in the repository.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
One dict, OFFSITE_BACKUP, in settings.py. Every key has a default; the backends each take a block of their own — BACKEND, a dotted path, plus that backend's options.

import os

OFFSITE_BACKUP = {
    'PREFIX': 'acme/prod',
    'ENV': 'prod',
    'NAME': 'acme',
    'STORE': {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.stores.s3.S3Store',
        'ENDPOINT_URL': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_ENDPOINT', ''),
        'REGION': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_REGION', ''),
        'BUCKET': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_BUCKET', ''),
        'ACCESS_KEY': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_ACCESS_KEY', ''),
        'SECRET_KEY': os.environ.get('BACKUP_S3_SECRET_KEY', ''),
        'LOCK_DAYS': 13,
    },
    'ENCRYPTION': {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.encryption.age_cli.AgeCli',
        'RECIPIENTS': os.environ.get('BACKUP_AGE_RECIPIENT', ''),
    },
    'DATABASES': {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.databases.postgres.PostgresSource',
        'ALIASES': ['default'],
        'FORMAT': 'plain',
    },
    'MEDIA': [
        {'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.media.filesystem.DirectorySource', 'EXCLUDE': ['thumbs/*']},
    ],
    'CONFIG': {
        'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.config.paths.PathsSource',
        'PATHS': ['/app/deploy'],
        'RENDER_ENV': 'deploy-vars.txt',
    },
    'RETENTION': {'KEEP_NIGHTS': 14},
    'CHECK': {'STALE_HOURS': 26},
    'NOTIFY': [
        {
            'BACKEND': 'offsite_backup.notifiers.telegram.TelegramNotifier',
            'TOKEN': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_TOKEN', ''),
            'CHAT_ID': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_CHAT_ID', ''),
            'TOPIC_ID': os.environ.get('BACKUP_TELEGRAM_TOPIC_ID', ''),
        },
    ],
    'GUARD': {'CACHE': 'default'},
}

Credentials come from the environment, in your settings. The package never reads os.environ for its configuration (the one exception is AGE_IDENTITY, the private key a restore reads — see Restore). Read each one with a default of '', as above: an unset variable then means "off", not a KeyError at import.

docs.title: ENABLED: off, on, or refused
docs.text:
Three states, never confused:

  • off — OFFSITE_BACKUP is absent or empty, ENABLED is false, or none of the options that name a destination is set. Commands print "not configured on this machine, nothing to do" and exit 0; the system checks say nothing. A development machine holds no key — not giving it one is the enforcement.
  • partly configured — something says "back up" and something it needs is empty. Every missing piece is named by E001, and a pass refuses to start. It is never read as "off": a production machine that lost one variable must not stop backing up in silence.
  • on — every backend builds and every required option is set.

With ENABLED left at None (the default) the machine is on when any of these is non-empty:

backend options that switch it on S3Store BUCKET, ACCESS_KEY, SECRET_KEY, ENDPOINT_URL DirectoryStore ROOT

A recipient is not among them: it is a public key, and writing it into settings must not switch on every machine that has no store key.

A BACKEND path that does not import also counts as "on", so E002 can say what is wrong with it. ENABLED: True or False overrides the rule either way.

A recipient hard-coded in settings switches every machine on

A public key is not a secret, so it is tempting to write RECIPIENTS: ['age1...'] straight into settings.py. That makes every machine that loads those settings — developer laptops and CI included — partly configured, and manage.py check reports E001 everywhere. Read the recipient from the environment like the credentials, or set ENABLED from an environment variable of its own.

docs.title: Top-level keys
docs.text:
Every key of offsite_backup.conf.DEFAULTS. RETENTION, CHECK and GUARD merge with their defaults key by key, so 'GUARD': {'CACHE': 'redis'} keeps RUNNING_SECONDS; every other key replaces its default whole.

key type default what it is validated by ENABLED bool or None None on/off; None decides from the options above — PREFIX str '' every key lives under <PREFIX>/; rotation never leaves it. Surrounding / are stripped. Required E001 ENV str '' the environment, for the message's hashtag (#prod) — NAME str '' a service name; shown in a message only when PREFIX is empty — STORE block None where backups are kept — S3 or a directory. Required E001, E002 ENCRYPTION block None how they are sealed — Encryption. Required E001, E002, E008 DATABASES block None Databases E001, E002 MEDIA list of blocks (or one block) [] Media E001, E002, W005 CONFIG block None Configuration archive E002, W005 COMPRESS list of str (argv) ['zstd', '-19', '--long=27', '-T0', '-q'] the compression stage for databases and the configuration archive; empty turns compression off E003 (zstd on PATH when non-empty) DECOMPRESS list of str (argv) ['zstd', '-d', '-q', '--long=31'] the stage a restore runs on anything that starts with zstd's magic bytes — RETENTION dict {'KEEP_NIGHTS': 14} Retention E001, E007 CHECK dict {'STALE_HOURS': 26} Monitoring — NOTIFY list of blocks [] Notifications E002, W004 MESSAGES dotted path 'offsite_backup.messages.default' the formatter — Notifications — GUARD dict see below the once-per-night claim — Scheduling E001, W003 LAST_SUCCESS_FILE path '' a file rewritten with the ISO time of every successful pass — Monitoring — WORKDIR path '' where the temporary workspace is made; '' is the system's temporary directory —

At least one of DATABASES, MEDIA and CONFIG must be set, or E001 says "nothing to back up".

docs.title: RETENTION
docs.text: key type default KEEP_NIGHTS positive int 14 whole UTC nights kept per kind. Must be greater than the store's LOCK_DAYS (E007); not a positive integer is E001

docs.title: CHECK
docs.text: key type default STALE_HOURS number 26 how old the newest whole backup may be before the morning check calls it missing

docs.title: GUARD
docs.text: key type default ENABLED bool True whether run_nightly() claims the night at all CACHE cache alias 'default' must exist in CACHES (E001) and be shared between workers (W003 on LocMemCache and DummyCache) RUNNING_SECONDS int 3600 how long a pass whose worker died holds the night DONE_SECONDS int 93600 (26 h) how long "done" is remembered — past the end of its UTC date

docs.title: Backend options
docs.text: Every backend reads its own block: BACKEND plus the options below. An option listed as required is named by E001 when empty on a machine where backups are on.

docs.title: STORE: offsite_backup.stores.s3.S3Store
docs.text:
Needs the [s3] extra. Stores: S3.

option type default BUCKET str — required ACCESS_KEY str — required SECRET_KEY str — required ENDPOINT_URL URL None (AWS) the provider's endpoint, e.g. https://fsn1.your-objectstorage.com REGION str None the region name the provider expects LOCK_DAYS int 13 days every object is locked COMPLIANCE; 0 stores without a lock. Checked against the bucket's default rule (E006) and against KEEP_NIGHTS (E007)

Only these options make the client: no ~/.aws, no instance role, no AWS_* variables.

docs.title: STORE: offsite_backup.stores.filesystem.DirectoryStore
docs.text:
Stores: directory. Always raises W001.

option type default ROOT path — required; ~ is expanded

docs.title: ENCRYPTION: offsite_backup.encryption.age_cli.AgeCli
docs.text:
Encryption. Runs age (E003).
